title: Structs
learningGoals: define a struct with several fields
make and fill a struct variable
pass a struct to a function

youtube.title: C++ Structs: Group Your Data | C++ Programming EP 51
youtube.description: In this episode you will define a struct with several fields, make and fill a struct variable and pass a struct to a function, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Structs · 0:49 A student struct · 1:29 Fields in memory · 1:59 Second program · 2:59 Recap · 3:29 Bug of the Day · 4:17 Challenge · 4:37 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "STRUCTS" in tomato on peach; Xecxec next to a student ID card with name and marks; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a student ID card with name and marks

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we make our own type. A struct groups related data, like the fields on an ID card.

scenes.onScreen: "Structs": numbered lines (1. A struct groups related variables; 2. Each variable is a field; 3. The dot reaches a field) and an analogy card: an ID card: one card, many fields
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A struct groups related variables under one name. Each variable inside is a field. You define the struct once, and then you make as many variables of it as you like. The dot operator reaches one field. Think of an ID card. It is one card, but it holds a name, a class and a number.

analogy.title: Structs
analogy.body: An ID card: one card, many fields

scenes.onScreen: student.cpp: a struct with a name and marks
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The struct has a name for the new type. [HL 6] The first field is a string. [HL 7] The second field is an int. [HL 8] Do not forget the semicolon after the closing brace. [HL 11] Here we make a variable of the new type. [HL 12] The dot reaches a field. We set the name. [HL 13] Then we set the marks. [HL 14] We print both fields.

scenes.onScreen: the struct s holds two fields, side by side
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the struct in memory. It has two fields. The name sits first, and the marks come next. The compiler may add small gaps between fields, to keep them aligned.

scenes.onScreen: list.cpp: a function takes a struct by const reference
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 10] The function takes a const reference, as in episode twenty-five. No copy is made. [HL 15] Braces fill the fields in order. Asha gets the name, and ninety-one gets the marks. [HL 16] Ravi has seventy-eight. [HL 17] We call show for each student. The output has two lines.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as list dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints Asha colon ninety-one, and then Ravi colon seventy-eight.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A struct groups related variables. Two. Each variable inside is a field. Three. The dot operator reaches a field. Four. Pass a big struct by const reference. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Each variable inside is a field.
The dot operator reaches a field.
Pass a big struct by const reference.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A missing semicolon after a struct
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The struct has no semicolon after its closing brace. The compiler says expected semicolon after struct definition. A struct is a declaration, so it needs a semicolon. This is one of the most common beginner errors.

scenes.onScreen: I made a struct for my fish. It has two fields: name and price. The price is always a catch.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I made a struct for my fish. It has two fields: name and price. The price is always a catch.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: make a book struct
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Make a struct called Book with a title and a price. Make two books and print them with a function. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: classes and objects. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.why: A struct definition is a declaration, and every declaration ends with a semicolon. The compiler reads on and gets confused.

pun: "I made a struct for my fish. It has two fields: name and price. The price is always a catch."
challenge: Make a struct called Book with a title and a price. Make two books and print them with a function.
challengeAnswer: Define struct Book with a string and a double. Write a show function with a const reference. Call it for both books.
